vignette:
He is fifty-one years old, a welder from an island nation in Oceania, now living in a coastal town that smells of salt and diesel. He has been married for twenty-seven years to a woman who still braids flowers into her hair on Sundays. He comes to therapy because she made the appointment. He says he is fine, just tired.

Three years ago, he was driving home from a job site on the coastal highway, a two-lane road that hugs the cliffs. It was late afternoon, the sun low and blinding. He was in his old flatbed truck, welding equipment rattling in the back. He remembers the other driver's headlights cutting across the lane like a fish hook. Then the metal scream, the smell of hot wiring and fuel, his own ribs pressing into the steering column. He was pinned for forty-five minutes. He remembers thinking, I will not see my wife again. A man from the village held his hand through the shattered window and told him to keep breathing.

Physically, he healed. Three broken ribs, a fractured clavicle, a deep gash on his forearm that left a scar like a seam. He went back to work six months later. But he no longer drives that highway. He takes the old inland road, which adds twenty minutes, but he says it feels safer. Sometimes he pulls over for no reason-a tightness in his chest, a ringing in his ears-and waits until his hands stop shaking.

At the welding shop, he is still skilled. His beads are clean, his torch steady. But sudden loud noises make him drop his visor. A car backfiring outside sends him into a crouch behind the workbench. The other welders have learned not to tap him on the shoulder from behind. He now works the later shift so he can leave after traffic clears. He does not tell them why.

At night, he sleeps in a separate room. He tells his wife it is because he sweats too much. In truth, he wakes two or three times from dreams of glass and fire. In the dream, he is still pinned, and the man holding his hand is gone, and the fuel is dripping. He wakes gasping, heart pounding, and does not want to wake her. She knows anyway. She has stopped asking.

He feels distant from his children, who are grown and live abroad. He does not call them. He does not know what to say. He used to fish on weekends with his brother-in-law. Now he stays home, walking the same short loop around the yard, checking the locks on the gate twice. He has not been to the beach in over a year. The sound of waves reminds him of the tide coming in under the wrecked truck, though the truck was nowhere near the water.

He tells me he does not think about the accident anymore. Then he sits in silence for a long time, rubbing the scar on his forearm. He says he feels hollow, like someone has scooped out the part of him that used to care about things. His wife says he has become irritable, that he snaps at small things-a misplaced tool, a cold dinner. He does not see it that way. He sees himself as tired.

He still goes to work. He still pays the bills. He still eats and sleeps and breathes. But he says there is a cord inside him that used to hum. Now it is quiet. He does not know how to find the hum again.
